intent_synonyms: How to name a character|What to call the protagonist|Choosing names|Fantasy personal names
model_instruction: Preserve cultivation atmosphere and classical imagery; avoid ordinary modern names and conspicuous puns.
summary: Fantasy names should evoke cultivation and classical culture rather than transplant everyday modern names.
details: Prefer classical single or compound surnames. Given names may evoke heaven, clouds, swords, or spirits; avoid duplicating major characters' names or breaking stylistic continuity.
rule: Balance recognizable individuality with cultivation imagery and the world's vocabulary.
positive_example: Xiao Yan, Ye Lingtian, Murong Ziyan
negative_example: Zhang Wei, Li Ming, Wang Xiaohua

intent_synonyms: Naming urban characters|Writing modern names|Choosing names
model_instruction: Follow realistic naming patterns and occupational character; avoid melodramatic classical names in modern scenes.
summary: Urban names should fit real life and social class, not sound like overblown fantasy.
details: A common surname with a moderately distinctive given name is reliable. Family background or unusual work can justify different naming conventions and tones.
rule: Match everyday life and personal identity; excessive classical grandeur undermines immersion.
positive_example: Chen Mo, Lin Wanqing, Gu Nancheng
negative_example: Shangguan Yichen, Murong Heavenly Emperor, Long Aotian

intent_synonyms: Choosing a book title|What to call a novel|Writing titles
model_instruction: Make the selling point and recognizability come before ornate wording.
summary: Keep titles short, precise, and informative enough to convey genre and central appeal at a glance.
details: In Chinese, aim for two to six characters or a short premise-driven phrase. Avoid excessive length, crowded information, or obscured central conflict.
rule: Be concise and forceful; convey the premise or world without sacrificing clarity for decoration.
positive_example: Battle Through the Heavens|Perfect World|My Heroic Husband
negative_example: The Story of What Happened After I Became the Strongest Person in Another World

intent_synonyms: Choosing volume titles|Writing arc titles|What to call each volume
model_instruction: Prioritize the stage's task and conflict before poetry; keep one naming register across the book.
summary: A volume title should signal its task, new location, or escalation so readers see how it differs from the previous volume.
details: Base long-series titles on growth stages, major settings, central enemies, or emotional arcs. Do not switch between unrelated aesthetic systems.
rule: Show progression and structural purpose; consistency matters more than a single flashy title.
positive_example: First Trial at the Sect|Undercurrents in the Imperial Capital|Battle for the North
negative_example: Volume One|Volume Two|Those Things

intent_synonyms: Choosing chapter titles|Writing chapter headings|Naming sections
model_instruction: Use a title to support suspense or a key event, not to announce routine activities.
summary: A good short chapter title identifies an event or a memorable suspense hook.
details: Use a character's action, an anomalous discovery, a key question, or a sharp judgment; avoid naming mundane daily actions.
rule: Be brief, clear, and enticing; emphasize what makes this chapter worth opening.
positive_example: He Has Returned|That Is Not Human Outside|Pier Seven
negative_example: Eating|Chatting|Another Day of Moving Forward

intent_synonyms: Inventing slang|Writing internal terminology|Naming dialect slang
model_instruction: Let jargon reflect group values and habitat; reserve it for key nouns instead of filling dialogue with invented words.
summary: Slang should suggest a group's culture, professional habits, or region and make its speech feel internally coherent.
details: Thieves' guilds, cyberpunk streets, and sect gangs can have distinctive jargon. Use it sparingly, especially for money, police, allies, and enemies.
rule: Make terms understandable, memorable, and culturally meaningful; novelty should not make reading needlessly difficult.
positive_example: Smokelings|Glints|Root-brothers
negative_example: QX-77 Interpersonal Collaboration Target Entity|Gibberish with no inferable meaning

intent_synonyms: Naming noble ranks|Naming offices|Writing titles
model_instruction: Match offices, ranks, and honorifics to powers and duties; use one cultural register rather than mixing traditions indiscriminately.
summary: Titles should reveal hierarchy, responsibilities, and cultural origins, not merely sound impressive.
details: A Chinese-style hierarchy can use duke, marquis, count, viscount, baron, minister, and military governor; Western fantasy should use its own coherent noble and knightly system rather than random combinations.
rule: Titles in one hierarchy must form a system that partly communicates power, territory, and obligations.
positive_example: Marquis Who Guards the North|Vice Minister of Rites|Knight Commander of the White Tower
negative_example: Duke-Minister-King|Archmage County Magistrate|Randomly spliced Eastern and Western titles

intent_synonyms: Naming myths|Writing divine epithets|Naming prophecy terms
model_instruction: Build a coherent symbolic system with recurring motifs such as sun, masks, eclipses, and chains.
summary: Memorable mythic names share stable symbols and a cultural register, as if they grew from one civilization.
details: Deities, artifacts, prophecy sections, and ancient places should share imagery such as light, scales, a broken moon, or seven locks rather than each receiving an unrelated cool name.
rule: Trace names to common cultural motifs that support later echoes and variations.
positive_example: God of the Golden Scales|Broken-Mask Prophet|Seven Locks Return the Night
negative_example: Sun God A|Dark Dragon Overlord|A collage of cool names with no cultural core

keywords: Premise-driven titles|direct titles|title click appeal|selling-point names
intent_synonyms: Putting the hook in the title|Making a webnovel title clear|Making titles clickable
model_instruction: Anchor the title in the strongest selling point; clarity beats an obscure name that pleases only the author.
summary: Direct premise titles work well in platform feeds because readers immediately see what the book offers.
details: System, rebirth, broken engagement, universal awakening, uncanny events, and invincibility are useful signals when paired with a real distinction; these often attract more clicks than purely poetic titles.
rule: Make genre and central payoff recognizable before polishing beauty and novelty.
positive_example: Everyone Changes Class: I Alone Have a Unique Passive|After My Engagement Ended, I Became the Empire's War God
negative_example: Wind on the Long Street|Pure imagery that reveals neither genre nor premise

intent_synonyms: Making a title intriguing|Choosing suspense titles|Leaving a hook
model_instruction: Leave a definite question rather than a pile of abstractions, and tie it tightly to the manuscript's central conflict.
summary: A suspense title should create an irresistible question, not merely pretend to be profound.
details: Who died, who returned, what lies behind the door, or why the bride changed at the wedding can drive curiosity, but the story must actually deliver.
rule: Use a concrete question linked to a high-conflict scene rather than empty mystery.
positive_example: My Dead First Love Returned on My Wedding Day|The Rules Say Never Open the Door, but My Mother Is Outside
negative_example: After the Secret|Apparently mysterious but offering no actual hook

intent_synonyms: Highlighting the protagonist in a title|Using an identity as a title|Titling with character traits
model_instruction: If the protagonist is the strongest selling point, foreground their identity, profession, or distinctive label.
summary: A character title works when the identity itself suggests genre and story expectations.
details: Forensic examiner, night watchman, disgraced holy son, Seventh-Sequence engineer, and amnesiac assassin all imply a narrative entry point.
rule: Use a distinctive identity that can sustain the whole book; do not pretend an ordinary occupation is inherently a hook.
positive_example: The Seventh Night Watchman|The Amnesiac Assassin Is Pretending to Be a Student Again
negative_example: An Ordinary Person|An identity with no distinction or genre promise

keywords: Worldbuilding titles|setting titles|large-scale setting names|world titles
intent_synonyms: Highlighting worldbuilding in a title|Naming setting-driven fiction|Putting the background in the title
model_instruction: When the world is the main distinction, anchor the title in a setting, rule, or civilization name.
summary: Setting-driven titles can sell the world before selling its characters.
details: The Dark Forest, Graveyard of Stars, Sea of the End, Seven Layers of School Rules, and Scripture of the Fog City draw readers into a distinctive world.
rule: Make the setting name vivid and recognizable, not understandable only to its creator.
positive_example: Fog City Containment Files|The Ninth Throne on the Sea of the End
negative_example: Project X Worldbuilding|A document label rather than a novel title

keywords: Timeline volume titles|stage titles|growth-stage naming|volume sequences
intent_synonyms: Ordering titles by growth stage|Unifying volume titles|Naming a chronology
model_instruction: Let the volume sequence show growth stages or turning points so readers locate each phase of life and conflict.
summary: Stage-based titles compress a sprawling novel into clear milestones.
details: Enrollment, first trials, expedition, a lost city, return, and coronation naturally suggest progression and reinforce whole-book structure.
rule: Keep one register and level of abstraction; do not alternate randomly among place names, poems, and slogans.
positive_example: First Steps in the North|Expedition Through the Long Night|The Royal City Burns|Return at Dawn
negative_example: Volume one is a place, two an idiom, and three an internet joke, with no shared style

keywords: Question chapter titles|interrogative titles|suspense headings|chapter hooks
intent_synonyms: Choosing question titles|Making chapter names intriguing|When to use a question heading
model_instruction: Compress the key new uncertainty into a short question, especially before a revelation or a reversal of understanding.
summary: A question title directs attention to the chapter's greatest unknown.
details: Who Is Outside?, Why Did She Smile?, and Who Changed the Rules? can provoke stronger onward curiosity than statements.
rule: Ask something concrete that the chapter meaningfully advances; do not use empty clickbait.
positive_example: Why Is He at the Funeral?|Who Crossed Out School Rule Seven?
negative_example: What Will Happen?|Too vague to create a definite expectation

intent_synonyms: Choosing four-character headings|Writing parallel titles|Making titles visually consistent
model_instruction: For concise or classical prose, use compact or parallel titles that fit the manuscript's tone.
summary: Four-character Chinese titles create a neat, dignified visual rhythm within a volume.
details: Clouds Rise, Winds Stir; Old Dreams, Layered Gates; A Sword Leaves the Northern Court; and Storms Approach are concise and vivid, but suit colloquial prose less well.
rule: Choose a compact phrase that captures the event's mood; do not force unfamiliar words merely to meet a count.
positive_example: An Old Lamp's Tiny Flame|Snow Presses on the City|Homeward Boat Beneath the Moon
negative_example: The Super-Ultimate Battle Has Begun|Too long and tonally inconsistent

intent_synonyms: Choosing numbered titles|When numbered titles fit|Making titles memorable
model_instruction: Use numbers only when they carry worldbuilding meaning, not merely to look fashionable.
summary: Numbers create memorable series identity when they matter to the plot.
details: Pier Seven, Apartment 404, Seven Layers of School Rules, and Containment Room Nine catch attention when anchored in real rules or places.
rule: Connect the number to the setting, rule hierarchy, or a key location rather than using arbitrary decoration.
positive_example: Apartment 404|School Rule Seven
negative_example: King of 10086|A number unrelated to the story, leaving only awkwardness

keywords: Poetic imagery titles|poetic titles|atmospheric titles|imagery naming
intent_synonyms: Making a title elegant|Creating poetic titles|Avoiding empty literary titles
model_instruction: Keep a poetic title attached to genre atmosphere or a central image rather than beautiful but empty words.
summary: Atmospheric titles should still suggest a genre, emotion, or thematic direction.
details: Moon, snow, fire, tides, night, ruined cities, and old dreams can anchor titles when they repeatedly echo worldbuilding or emotional motifs.
rule: Use stable imagery that resonates with the story's themes, not two randomly attractive words.
positive_example: Snow Falls on the Long Street|The Lamp Beyond the Sea of Mist
negative_example: Wind Flowers Moon Dreams|Empty word-stacking with neither genre nor a memorable point

intent_synonyms: Building contrast into titles|Making titles eye-catching|Choosing contrasting titles
model_instruction: Make both sides of the contrast clear so conflict is immediate; do not simply pair unrelated words.
summary: Contrast titles collide the protagonist's circumstances with an anomaly.
details: Failure versus genius, pauper versus tycoon, ex-partner versus wedding, and rules versus family are strong attention-grabbing structures.
rule: Make the contrast serve the main premise and conflict so readers see where the tension comes from.
positive_example: The Whole School Thinks I Am Useless|After the Divorce, My Ex Begged Me to Return
negative_example: Black and White|Abstract opposition without a story hook

keywords: Emotionally resonant titles|emotional titles|regret titles|resonance naming
intent_synonyms: Making a title moving|Writing emotional titles|Naming for resonance
model_instruction: Embed the relationship or regret most likely to touch the target reader instead of generic sadness.
summary: Emotional titles illuminate recognizable regret, missed opportunities, or obsession rather than merely sounding literary.
details: Divorce, secret love, reunion, broken promises, farewell, and forgiveness invite identification when tied to a specific relationship.
rule: Ground emotion in a relationship and event; sadness alone is not a story entrance.
positive_example: After the Divorce, I Finally Stopped Waiting for You|In the End, Neither of Us Looked Back
negative_example: Sad Memories|General emotion without characters or conflict

keywords: Mystery-statement titles|declarative suspense titles|anomalous-event titles|uncanny naming
intent_synonyms: Writing mystery titles without questions|Titling anomalous events|Making horror titles compelling
model_instruction: State an anomalous fact so readers encounter an impossible result and enter the story seeking its explanation.
summary: The technique presents a clearly wrong fact instead of asking a question.
details: The seventh corpse has no shadow, a stranger's name appears in school rules, or a dead person signs the wedding register creates firmer intrigue than an empty question mark.
rule: Make the anomaly concrete and strange enough to change expectations of the story.
positive_example: The Seventh Corpse Has No Shadow|The School Rules Give the Date of My Death
negative_example: A Secret Descends|Pretended mystery without a real anomaly

keywords: Geographic volume titles|map titles|class-based titles|migration titles
intent_synonyms: Showing a new location in volume titles|Naming a change of setting|Naming social-class stages
model_instruction: When volumes differ mainly by place, class, or social circle, name the new stage directly.
summary: Geographic and class-based titles quickly show what new world and rules the protagonist encounters.
details: Outer City, Inner Court, Northern Border, Upper District, Deep-Sea Station, and Second Academy imply new orders and enemies.
rule: Make the location or class correspond to the volume's central conflict, not a casually changed map label.
positive_example: Surviving the Outer City|The Imperial Capital's Chessboard|Deep-Sea Station Restricted Zone
negative_example: Went Somewhere New|A note rather than a formal title

keywords: Enemy volume titles|opponent titles|boss volume titles|antagonist-centered titles
intent_synonyms: Naming a volume after an enemy|One boss per volume|Highlighting an opponent
model_instruction: When a formidable opponent dominates the volume, name the enemy, faction, or title to emphasize the stage's confrontation.
summary: An opponent title identifies the pressure source and the obstacle this arc must overcome.
details: White Tower Inquisitor, Demon Queen of the Northern Sea, Red-Armored Army, and Fog City Priest can each anchor a volume.
rule: The opponent must sustain a whole volume and represent a substantial confrontation, not a disposable roadside monster.
positive_example: The White Tower Inquisitor|Demon Queen of the Northern Sea|The Red-Armored Army Arrives
negative_example: A Minor Villain Appears|An unimportant enemy forced into the volume title

keywords: X-of-Y titles|possessive chapter titles|classical chapter titles|template titles
intent_synonyms: Creating X-of-Y chapter titles|When possessive titles fit|Classical title templates
model_instruction: Use a compact possessive structure to capture mood and event, with a meaningful relationship between its two parts.
summary: The structure is stable, balanced, and easy to repeat consistently across a volume.
details: A Boy's Anger, The Person Beneath the Lamp, The Night of Return, and The Winter of Broken Promises combine classical flavor with events.
rule: Both parts must jointly point to the chapter's main event or emotion rather than fill a format mechanically.
positive_example: The Person Beneath the Lamp|The Night of Return|A Boy's Anger
negative_example: The Vastness of the World|Too broad to identify this chapter's content

keywords: Chapter subtitles|title and subtitle|secondary headings|two-part titles
intent_synonyms: Adding a chapter subtitle|When two-part titles fit|Combining information and atmosphere
model_instruction: Let the title capture the event and the subtitle add atmosphere or a condition; do not repeat the same meaning.
summary: A subtitle can add an emotional, geographic, or conditional layer to the main event.
details: The Eve of Battle (No One Slept) and A Letter from an Old Friend—But the Sender Is Dead fit information-rich pivotal chapters.
rule: Give each part a distinct job: main event first, only the most necessary additional information second.
positive_example: The Eve of Battle (No One Slept)|A Letter from an Old Friend—But the Sender Is Dead
negative_example: Battle Begins (The Battle Has Started)|Repetition without additional value

intent_synonyms: Naming cities and places|Choosing landmark names|Naming map locations
model_instruction: Express terrain, historical function, or cultural origins so readers sense why the place has its name.
summary: Good place names grow from landscape, history, resources, or a faction's traces rather than random attractive words.
details: Blacktide Harbor, Redstone Ridge, Old Royal City, and Cloudwalk Pass imply terrain or history and make maps memorable and credible.
rule: Connect names to geography, history, or practical functions rather than generic mobile-game locations.
positive_example: Blacktide Harbor|Old Royal City|Cloudwalk Pass
negative_example: Mysterious Place|Cool City|Neither origin nor distinction

intent_synonyms: Naming organizations|Naming sects and factions|Making a faction name credible
model_instruction: Show values, trade, or history so the name immediately conveys a stance and character.
summary: Strong names imply both beliefs and functions, suggesting how members act.
details: White Tower Council, Redfeather Battalion, Order of Returning Night, and Long Street Alliance suggest institutions, occupations, or faith.
rule: Align names with organizational nature, cultural register, and power structure instead of mixing eras and cultures randomly.
positive_example: White Tower Council|Redfeather Battalion|Order of Returning Night
negative_example: Mysterious Awesome Organization|Only the author thinks it is cool; readers cannot infer its nature

intent_synonyms: Naming techniques|Making skill names impressive|Avoiding tacky spell names
model_instruction: Show approach, effect, or origin; do not make every skill a stack of heavenly, demonic, divine, dragon, or world-destroying words.
summary: Useful technique names suggest how they work and why they are powerful rather than producing empty verbal explosions.
details: Tide-Cutting Step, Abyssal Return Seal, Bone-Burning Art, and Ninefold Thunder Spear communicate movement, elements, or lineage.
rule: Show at least one school, movement, element, cost, or inheritance instead of a uniform ultimate-attack voice.
positive_example: Tide-Cutting Step|Bone-Burning Art|Ninefold Thunder Spear
negative_example: Invincible Cosmic Divine Dragon World-Destroying Slash|Stacked grandiosity without a coherent system

keywords: Artifact names|relic names|divine-item names|key prop names
intent_synonyms: Naming artifacts|Giving relic names a story|Writing divine-item names
model_instruction: Give key objects both function and history, suggesting origins, costs, and old events.
summary: Memorable artifact and relic names draw on purpose, former owner, or symbolism.
details: Broken-Moon Lamp, Bone-Returning Casket, Judgment Ring, and Old King's Seal sound like objects and entrances into history.
rule: Do not name all objects in one style; the more important the object, the more closely name and narrative function should interlock.
positive_example: Broken-Moon Lamp|Bone-Returning Casket|Old King's Seal
negative_example: Super Artifact Number One|A temporary placeholder without a story

intent_synonyms: Choosing codenames|Making nicknames formidable|Numbered secret identities
model_instruction: Derive aliases from exploits, habits, rumors, or functions so they feel bestowed by others rather than self-proclaimed.
summary: A convincing alias sounds passed from person to person and implies why its bearer is known.
details: Gray Crow, Needle Seven, Corpse Collector, and White Gloves feel more lived-in than grand self-declarations.
rule: Keep names short, transmissible, and rumor-laden, reflecting methods, style, or a defining exploit.
positive_example: Gray Crow|Needle Seven|White Gloves
negative_example: Supreme God of Destruction|Childishly self-appointed, with no believable social origin

intent_synonyms: Naming career paths|Ordering sequence titles|Making advanced classes coherent
model_instruction: Keep a recognizable progression from low to high rank rather than making every stage feel like a different world.
summary: Vertical consistency shows where a path begins and how it develops.
details: Apprentice Night Patrolman, Night Watchman, Lamp Officer, and Chief Night Warden form a clearer chain than unrelated ranks.
rule: Share motifs or functional vocabulary so promotion feels like advancement, not random renaming.
positive_example: Apprentice Night Patrolman|Night Watchman|Lamp Officer
negative_example: Level one Hunter, level two Holy Son, level three Administrator|A completely disconnected path

intent_synonyms: Naming dungeons|Making realm names frightening|Making level titles compelling
model_instruction: Capture a central fear, rule, or anomalous scene so readers anticipate the kind of danger.
summary: Dungeon and secret-realm names should sell atmosphere and rules before ornate wording.
details: Unlit Schoolhouse, Seventh Aquarium, Echo Hospital, and Bone-Burial Corridor establish place and unease.
rule: Anchor the name to a definite setting image or rule-based fear rather than another generic Secret Realm.
positive_example: Unlit Schoolhouse|Echo Hospital|Bone-Burial Corridor
negative_example: Ultimate Dungeon|God-Tier Secret Realm|Too generic to create specific expectations

intent_synonyms: Naming bonus stories|Giving a finale resonance|Writing epilogue headings
model_instruction: Let endings and bonus-story titles provide closure and aftertaste rather than cold labels such as Extra One and Extra Two.
summary: These titles should offer an emotional landing point and begin the act of closing the story.
details: Years Later, After the Snow Stopped, The Lamp Is Still Lit, and A Letter from an Old Friend carry endings and later lives better than numbers.
rule: Emphasize closure, aftermath, or the direction of characters' lives instead of mechanically continuing ordinary serial headings.
positive_example: After the Snow Stopped|Years Later|A Letter from an Old Friend
negative_example: Extra One|Final Chapter 2|Administrative numbering without emotional value

intent_synonyms: Naming families|Writing bloodline titles|Naming noble houses
model_instruction: Show inheritance, region, or totemic origins before nobility; do not call every family a Heavenly Clan.
summary: A lineage name should carry history, geography, or a totem that suggests the traditions behind the surname.
details: Use mountains, seas, objects, ancestral teachings, totems, or founding lands rather than stacking holy, divine, and imperial.
rule: Reflect lineage and a common cultural register; every aristocratic house should not use a different linguistic system.
positive_example: Dantai Clan|Ancient Clan of Candle Mountain|Wenren of the White Deer
negative_example: Invincible Heavenly God Family|Supreme Imperial Clan X

intent_synonyms: Choosing plan codenames|Naming operations|Naming secret missions
model_instruction: Suggest the objective or cover story rather than relying on cool letters and forceful words.
summary: A good codename lets insiders remember its purpose without necessarily revealing it to outsiders.
details: Locations, weather, seasons, colors, or old allusions can provide cover while secretly mapping to the objective.
rule: Keep names short, speakable, and capable of secrecy or misdirection, not as long as project-document titles.
positive_example: Project Returning Tide|White Tower Clearance|Operation Black Rain
negative_example: Top-Secret Final Strongest Plan|A1B2C3Z9 with no meaning

keywords: Shop names|base names|tavern names|inn names|headquarters naming
intent_synonyms: Naming shops|Naming bases|Naming taverns and inns
model_instruction: Combine commercial function with personality; do not make every shop another Pavilion or Residence.
summary: Readers should infer what a place offers, its character, and why people remember it.
details: Taverns, apothecaries, black-market shops, investigation offices, and safe houses can draw names from owners' habits, neighborhoods, merchandise, or old epithets.
rule: Connect the name to function, location, or the owner's personality instead of an empty classical shell.
positive_example: Seven Lamps Tavern|Spring-Restoring Apothecary|Old Bridge Agency
negative_example: God's Shop|Supreme Pavilion 888

intent_synonyms: Naming trials|Naming contests|Naming sect tournaments
model_instruction: State the level and core test before chasing epic grandeur or intimidation.
summary: Selection criteria, danger level, and organizer style help establish the world's order.
details: Outer Sect Tournament, Hundred Towers Trial, Deep-Sea Recruitment Exam, and Winter Capital Selection communicate setting, purpose, and prestige.
rule: Include rank, venue, or function so readers can distinguish a festival, elimination event, or lethal trial.
positive_example: Hundred Towers Trial|Winter Capital Selection|Third Academy Joint Examination
negative_example: Strongest Competition|Ultimate Trial Contest Contest Contest

intent_synonyms: Writing rule headings|Naming laws|Naming horror rules
model_instruction: Make rule names clear before making them uncanny; readers must remember them before noticing the anomaly.
summary: Rule and law names need to be retold, quoted, and echoed through the story.
details: Silence Ordinance, After-Lights-Out Passage Regulations, and Seventh-Floor Care Rules combine administrative tone with implied danger better than abstract laws.
rule: Use short names anchored in a scene or behavior, with a slight anomaly rather than random frightening sentences.
positive_example: Silence Ordinance|Seventh-Floor Care Rules|Night Patrol Avoidance Law
negative_example: Never Trust Anyone or You Know What Will Happen|Too long to quote consistently

keywords: Result-first chapter titles|outcome-first headings|spoiler hooks|outcome titles
intent_synonyms: Giving the result in a title|Writing spoiler-style headings|Making chapter names gripping
model_instruction: Present an unusual outcome first and explain its process in the chapter without exposing the decisive secret.
summary: In high-conflict chapters, an already-completed result makes readers ask how it happened.
details: She Came After All, The Wedding Was Canceled, and Pier Seven Is Burning expose the situation, then gain impact through explanation.
rule: Choose a concrete, anomalous result that provokes why, not a routine announcement.
positive_example: The Wedding Was Canceled|She Came After All|Pier Seven Is Burning
negative_example: Something Happened|An outcome with no specificity

keywords: Command chapter titles|warning headings|imperative titles|do not open the door
intent_synonyms: Choosing command titles|Writing warning titles|Using do-not titles
model_instruction: Make the heading sound like a warning torn directly from the world's rules: short, forceful, and consequential.
summary: Imperatives create pressure and rules, fitting danger thresholds, triggered prohibitions, and reversals of understanding.
details: Do Not Look Back, Turn Off the Light First, and Do Not Say Her Name immediately place readers under a threatening rule.
rule: Use executable actions and definite objects, not vague commands or slogans.
positive_example: Do Not Look Back|Turn Off the Light First|Do Not Say Her Name
negative_example: Please Everyone Think Seriously About Life|Not a chapter hook

keywords: Evolving-motif volume titles|progressive imagery|series naming systems|consistent volume titles
intent_synonyms: Progressing titles across volumes|Sharing one motif|Ordering series titles
model_instruction: Vary one motif so every volume belongs to the same family while showing escalation.
summary: An evolving motif gives a long series aesthetic unity and structural order.
details: For a lamp motif, progress through lighting, guarding, burning, extinguishing, and relighting; this unifies titles while carrying growth and changes in the situation.
rule: Maintain one motif, abstraction level, and linguistic style so titles progress without tonal jumps.
positive_example: Night of Lighting Lamps|City of Guarded Lamps|Winter of Burning Lamps
negative_example: Volume One: Northern Border|Volume Two: Poems of Fate|Volume Three: Hit Them Hard|No coherent system

keywords: Region names|neighborhood names|district names|map layers|zone names
intent_synonyms: Naming map regions|Writing district names|Naming neighborhood strata
model_instruction: Prioritize function, class, or danger so readers immediately understand the local ecosystem.
summary: Compress a district's purpose, class character, or historical nickname into its name.
details: Lower City, Old Harbor District, Red Lantern Alley, and Gray Well Level supply setting information on first mention.
rule: Connect the name to geography, industry, class, or an old event instead of generic East Zone One and West Zone Two.
positive_example: Old Harbor District|Gray Well Level|Glazed Lantern Street
negative_example: Zone A1|New Place Number One|No atmosphere or functional information

keywords: Organization names|faction names|power-group names|camp names|gang names
intent_synonyms: Naming organizations|Naming factions|Making faction names coherent
model_instruction: Encode a source of power, operational style, or belief motif; do not call every group another Alliance or Association.
summary: Names should reveal what sustains the group, its style, and its cultural system.
details: Tribunal, Night Patrol Office, White Tower Council, and Red Tide Gang establish function and character better than abstract grandeur.
rule: Link names to power structures, methods, or origins, maintaining a common linguistic register within a system.
positive_example: White Tower Council|Night Patrol Office|Red Tide Gang
negative_example: Strongest Organization Alliance|Empty and trite, with no identity information

keywords: Protocol names|treaty names|act names|plan-document names|institutional names
intent_synonyms: Naming treaties|Writing protocol names|Naming acts and plans
model_instruction: Show what is regulated and the central provision rather than chasing a flashy codename.
summary: Clear institutional names make later references and conflicts more powerful.
details: After-Lights-Out Passage Ordinance, Sea-Mist Armistice Agreement, and Deep-Level Sample Sealing Act combine function with worldbuilding.
rule: Name the object, setting, and central restriction first; add official or historical tone only where needed.
positive_example: Sea-Mist Armistice Agreement|Deep-Level Sample Sealing Act|Night Navigation Avoidance Ordinance
negative_example: Ultimate Protocol|Sounds grand but does not say what it governs

keywords: Ranking-list names|leaderboard names|title systems|ranking names|honor rolls
intent_synonyms: Naming rankings|Choosing leaderboard names|Naming a title system
model_instruction: State the evaluation dimension and social prestige before pursuing grandeur.
summary: When readers know what is compared and who recognizes the standard, publication and competition become dramatic.
details: Wanted List, Constellation Ranking, Rising Cloud List, and Black-Gold Seats imply an evaluative arena and social weight.
rule: Consider the judging body, comparison criteria, and memorability; unfamiliar words should not create needless barriers.
positive_example: Rising Cloud List|Black-Gold Seats|Seven Cities Wanted List
negative_example: Cosmic Supergod Supreme Ranking|Piled-up words without institutional order

keywords: Final-chapter titles|title callbacks|circular headings|closure naming|finale titles
intent_synonyms: Naming the finale|Echoing the book title in the ending|Creating circular titles
model_instruction: A title callback must return to the central motif or opening promise rather than mechanically repeat the book's name.
summary: The most effective callback makes readers realize the journey has reached the opening's previously hidden meaning.
details: Echo an opening line, central image, or title keyword so the final heading itself creates closure and resonance.
rule: Do not simply copy: return to the motif with new meaning so the title gains a second illumination.
